Our final benchmark tests whether large language models (LLMs) can infer emotion labels from narrative text via direct prompting. For each sentence, we prompt the model with a standardized query that includes the highlighted character and asks for a list of emotions the character is feeling.

To evaluate the quality of these top-k predictions, we apply EMER-style set-based overlap metrics. Let Ŷ denote the set of predicted emotion labels for a given sentence and Y the set of gold labels aggregated across annotators. We compute set accuracy as Accuracy , the proportion of predicted labels that match the gold set, and set recall as Recall s = | Ŷ ∩Y | |Y | , the proportion of gold labels recovered by the model.

To validate the reliability of our citizen science approach, we conducted an expert validation study using a random sample of 100 passages [...] independently annotated by the four trained moderators [...] We employed linear mixed-effects models to compare expert assessments with citizen scientist annotations across three emotional dimensions—valence, arousal, and dominance.

To validate the reliability of our citizen science approach, we conducted an expert validation study using a random sample of 100 passages drawn from our dataset that had been annotated by at least four citizen scientists. These passages were then independently annotated by the four trained moderators of the project using the same interface and open-response format.

The four moderators are undergraduate students at McGill who participated in the project design, testing, and moderation for this and prior Citizen Reader projects.
